lesson.text: Quick memory: does fair always mean everyone gets exactly the same? (Not always: fair can mean everyone gets what they need.) Today we think about a big question together.
A big question is one that thoughtful people answer in different ways. “What is fair?” is one. “Is it ever fine to break a rule?” is another. There is no answer at the back of the book!
When we talk about a big question, we give a reason: “I think… because…” A reason helps others understand your view, even if they do not agree.
We listen carefully and can agree or disagree kindly: “I agree with Zara, and I would add…” or “I see it differently from Bram, because…” We disagree with ideas, never unkindly with people.
Try this one: Mimi baked 12 biscuits for 4 friends. Is 3 each fair? What if one friend helped to bake? What if one had no breakfast? Each idea of fair has its reason.
Three ideas of fair: everyone gets the same; people get what they need; people get more for more work. Which fits best can change with the situation.
Good thinkers can change their minds when they hear a good reason. That is not a defeat: it is learning!
Try it in the world: build a round table in your world and invite friends. Ask a big question, like “What makes a game fair?” Everyone gives a reason, and everyone listens.

exercises.hint: A big question has no single answer that everyone agrees on.
choices: How many legs has a cat?
exercises.explain: “What is fair?” is a big question: thoughtful people answer it in different ways.

choices: I think it is fair because we all helped.
exercises.explain: It gives a reason (because we all helped), so others can understand the view.

exercises.prompt: People can think different things about a big question.
exercises.hint: Is there an answer at the back of the book?
exercises.explain: True: big questions have more than one thoughtful answer.

exercises.prompt: When you disagree, it is fine to be unkind to the person.
exercises.hint: Do we disagree with ideas or with people?
exercises.explain: False: we can disagree with an idea and still be kind to the person.

exercises.prompt: What is a kind way to disagree?
exercises.hint: It should give a reason and be kind.
exercises.explain: Saying you see it differently, and why, is kind and helps the talk go on.

exercises.prompt: Mimi shares 12 biscuits equally among 4 friends. How many does each get?
exercises.hint: Share them out one by one, or think: 4 times what makes 12?

exercises.prompt: Zara gives more water to the thirstiest runner. Which idea of fair is that?
exercises.explain: The thirstiest runner needed more, so this is fair as giving people what they need.

exercises.prompt: Changing your mind after hearing a good reason is part of good thinking.
exercises.explain: True: good thinkers change their minds when they hear a good reason.

exercises.prompt: Tilly laid 8 blocks of a wall and Bram laid 2. They earned 10 gold. Which idea of fair gives Tilly 8 gold?
exercises.hint: Tilly did more of the work.
exercises.explain: Giving Tilly 8 gold for 8 blocks is fair as more reward for more work.

exercises.prompt: If Tilly and Bram share the 10 gold equally instead, how much does each get?
exercises.hint: Equal means the same for each. Halve 10.

exercises.prompt: Why do we give reasons for our views?
exercises.hint: Think of how a reason helps the listener.
choices: so others can understand and think about them
exercises.explain: A reason helps others understand your view and decide what they think of it.

exercises.prompt: A big question always has one right answer that everyone agrees on.
exercises.hint: Remember what makes a question big.
exercises.explain: False: big questions have many thoughtful answers, each with its reasons.

exercises.prompt: In a race, one runner starts halfway along. Why do many people say it is unfair?
exercises.hint: Think about each runner's chance to win.
choices: the runners did not have an equal chance
exercises.explain: A fair race gives everyone the same chance; a head start takes that away.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea of fair to an example of it.
exercises.hint: Look at who gets what in each example, and why.
exercises.explain: 3 biscuits each is the same for all; more water for the thirstiest is by need; 8 gold for 8 blocks is more for more work.

exercises.prompt: Which of these give a reason?
items: It's fair because she helped bake.
Fair means the same, so 3 each.
exercises.hint: Look for because, or for so: they join an idea to its reason.
exercises.explain: “Because she helped bake” and “so 3 each” are reasons. “It's fair” and “just because” give none.

exercises.prompt: Put a good talk about a big question in order.
items: Listen to the next person's view.
exercises.hint: First your view, then why, then someone else has a turn.
exercises.explain: Say what you think, give your reason, then listen to the next person's view.

exercises.prompt: Sort the examples by their idea of fair.
items: one turn each on the swing
a bigger share for the baker
exercises.hint: Is everyone treated the same, is it about what someone needs, or is it about the work they did?
exercises.explain: The same for all: 3 biscuits each, one turn each. What each needs: water for the thirstiest, a ramp for a wheelchair. More for more work: 8 gold for 8 blocks, a bigger share for the baker.

exercises.prompt: Mimi baked 12 biscuits. Ava helped, so she gets 2 extra. The other 10 are shared equally among 5 friends, Ava too. How many does Ava get?
exercises.hint: Share the 10 equally first, then add Ava's extra 2.
exercises.explain: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 each. Ava gets her 2 and 2 extra for helping: 2 + 2 = 4 biscuits. This mixes two ideas of fair: the same for all, and more for more work.

exercises.prompt: Order a good talk about "Is it ever fine to break a rule?"
items: Change your mind if a reason is good.
exercises.hint: A talk starts with the question, and good thinkers listen before they decide.
exercises.explain: Ask the big question, give your view with a reason, listen to others and disagree kindly, and be ready to change your mind when you hear a good reason.
